procedural_history.originating_court: Magistrate Court (order affirmed by Sessions Court in revision)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Orders of the Magistrate Court (affirmed by the Sessions Court) regarding interim compensation
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The orders of the Magistrate and Sessions Courts were challenged before the High Court of Jharkhand at Ranchi in CRMP No. 836 of 2021. The High Court dismissed the petition in a judgment dated 03.01.2023.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant(s) approached the Supreme Court challenging the High Court's judgment that upheld the orders regarding interim compensation. The Supreme Court set aside the orders and directed the Trial Court to consider the application for grant of interim compensation afresh.

directions: The orders of the courts below are set aside.
The Trial Court is directed to consider the application for grant of interim compensation afresh.

issue.issue_text: Whether the provision of sub-section (1) of Section 143A of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, which provides for the grant of interim compensation, is mandatory.

facts: The case concerned whether Section 143A(1) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, which allows a court to order the drawer of a cheque to pay interim compensation to the complainant, is a mandatory or a discretionary provision.

The appellant argued that the use of the word 'may' in the statute indicates that the power is discretionary and requires the court to apply its mind to the facts, including the existence of a prima facie case, before issuing such an order.

The respondent contended that the provision must be treated as mandatory to fulfill the objective of the Act and that the presumption under Section 139 of the Act justifies ordering interim compensation in every case.
law: Section 143A(1) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, states that a court trying an offence under Section 138 'may' order the drawer of the cheque to pay interim compensation.

The court considered the legal principle that interpreting a provision as mandatory can have drastic consequences and may raise constitutional concerns regarding fairness, justice, and arbitrariness under Article 14 of the Constitution.
application: The Supreme Court focused on the word 'may' used in Section 143A(1) and refused to interpret it as 'shall'.

The Court reasoned that treating the provision as mandatory would have 'drastic consequences,' forcing an accused to pay up to 20% of the cheque amount in every case before any adjudication of guilt. This was deemed 'unjust and contrary to the well-settled concept of fairness and justice.'
A mandatory interpretation, the Court noted, could expose the provision to being struck down as 'manifestly arbitrary' and unconstitutional.

The Court established that the power is discretionary and must not be exercised mechanically. Before ordering interim compensation, the trial court must conduct a prima facie evaluation of the merits of both the complainant's case and the defense pleaded by the accused.

The Court clarified that the statutory presumption under Section 139 is not, by itself, a sufficient ground to order interim compensation, as the presumption is rebuttable and applies at the trial stage.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the provision for granting interim compensation under Section 143A(1) of the Negotiable Instruments Act is directory, not mandatory. The court's power to order such compensation is discretionary and must be exercised only after applying its mind to the prima facie merits of the case, rather than being granted automatically.

issue.issue_text: Whether the court must consider factors such as the prima facie case before exercising its discretionary power to grant interim compensation under Section 143A(1) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881.

facts: The case involved a criminal appeal concerning an order for the accused to pay interim compensation under Section 143A of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881.
The Trial Court had ordered the accused to deposit Rs. 10,00,000 as interim compensation.
The Supreme Court found that the lower courts had passed this order 'mechanically' without proper application of mind to the facts of the case.
law: Section 143A(1) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, states that a court 'may' order the drawer of a cheque to pay interim compensation to the complainant.
The Court interpreted the word 'may' as conferring a discretionary (directory) power, not a mandatory one.

The Court reasoned that interpreting 'may' as 'shall' (mandatory) would have drastic and unjust consequences, forcing an accused to pay up to 20% of the cheque amount in every case before guilt is proven, which could be arbitrary and violate Article 14 of the Constitution.
application: Since the power under Section 143A(1) is discretionary, the Court held that it cannot be exercised automatically or mechanically.
The deciding court must apply its mind and conduct a prima facie evaluation of the merits of both the complainant's case and the accused's defense.
A direction to pay interim compensation can only be issued if the complainant makes out a prima facie case.
The court cannot rely solely on the rebuttable presumption under Section 139 of the Act to order compensation.
If the accused's defense is found to be 'prima facie plausible,' the court has the discretion to refuse the grant of interim compensation.

If the court decides to grant compensation, it must also apply its mind to the quantum (amount), considering factors like the nature of the transaction, the relationship between the parties, and the financial distress of the accused.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that a court must consider several factors, including the existence of a prima facie case made by the complainant and the plausibility of the defense raised by the accused, before exercising its discretionary power to grant interim compensation under Section 143A(1) of the Negotiable Instruments Act. The power is directory, not mandatory, and requires a reasoned application of mind rather than a mechanical order.

issue.issue_text: Whether the tests applicable for the exercise of jurisdiction under Section 148(1) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, should also apply to the exercise of power under Section 143A(1).

law.fact: Section 148(1) of the Negotiable Instruments Act applies at the appellate stage, after an accused person has already been convicted following a full trial.
law.source: Held: Sub-section (1) of s.148 confers on the Appellate Court a power to direct the appellant/accused to deposit 20 per cent of the compensation amount – It operates at a different level as the power thereunder can be exercised only after the appellant/accused is convicted after a full trial.

law.fact: Section 143A(1) of the Negotiable Instruments Act applies at the trial stage, before the accused has been found guilty. It allows a court to order the payment of interim compensation.
law.source: In the case of s.143A, the power can be exercised even before the accused is held guilty.

law.fact: The power under Section 143A(1) is discretionary ('may') and not mandatory ('shall') because it is a drastic measure that penalizes an accused before guilt is established.
law.source: s.143A can be invoked before the conviction of the accused, and therefore, the word “may” used therein can never be construed as “shall”.

application.fact: The Court reasoned that the two sections operate at completely different levels and stages of the legal process.
application.source: It operates at a different level as the power thereunder can be exercised only after the appellant/accused is convicted after a full trial – In the case of s.143A, the power can be exercised even before the accused is held guilty.

application.fact: An order under Section 148 is made against a person already convicted, while an order under Section 143A is made against a person who is still presumed innocent.
application.source: Sub-section (1) of Section 143A provides for passing a drastic order for payment of interim compensation against the accused in a complaint under Section 138, even before any adjudication is made on the guilt of the accused.

application.fact: Because of this fundamental difference in the timing and context of their application, the legal tests and considerations for one cannot be applied to the other.
application.source: The tests applicable for the exercise of jurisdiction under sub-section (1) of Section 148 can never apply to the exercise of jurisdiction under sub-section (1) of Section 143A of the N.I. Act.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the proposition, holding that the tests for exercising power under Section 148(1) cannot apply to Section 143A(1). The Court's reasoning was based on the fundamental difference between the two sections: Section 148 applies post-conviction at the appellate stage, whereas Section 143A applies pre-conviction at the trial stage. Therefore, they operate at entirely different levels, and the considerations for each are distinct.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the provision of sub-section (1) of Section 143A of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, which provides for the grant of interim compensation, is mandatory.
appellant_arguments: The provision for granting interim compensation under Section 143A(1) is not mandatory but is a discretionary power of the court.
respondent_arguments: The provision for granting interim compensation under Section 143A(1) is mandatory, and the court is bound to grant it if the conditions are met.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the court must consider factors such as the prima facie case before exercising its discretionary power to grant interim compensation under Section 143A(1) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881.
appellant_arguments: The court must exercise its discretion judiciously by evaluating the merits of the case, including the case made out by the complainant, the defence pleaded by the accused, and the financial distress of the accused.
respondent_arguments: A detailed evaluation of the merits is not required at the interim stage, as the purpose of the section is to provide prompt relief to the complainant.

cases.case_name: Surinder Singh Deswal v. Virender Gandhi
cases.principle: A purposive interpretation should be made of Section 148 of the NI Act, and while an appellate court is normally justified in imposing a condition of deposit, an exception can be made for recorded reasons if the condition is unjust or would deprive the appellant of the right to appeal.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: While an appellate court should normally impose the condition of a deposit as provided in Section 148 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, it has the discretion to make an exception if it is satisfied that the condition would be unjust or would deprive the appellant of the right to appeal, provided that specific reasons for such an exception are recorded.
obiter: The word 'may' ordinarily does not mean 'must', but this is not an inflexible rule; its interpretation depends on the nature of the power, legislative intent, and the context in which it is used.
The factors for determining whether to grant an exception to the deposit requirement are not exhaustive and other relevant factors may exist in the peculiar facts of a given case.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The power granted to a court under sub-section (1) of Section 143A of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, to direct the payment of interim compensation is discretionary and not mandatory. The use of the word "may" in the provision does not mean "must" or "shall". Consequently, the court must exercise this discretion judiciously by conducting a prima facie evaluation of the merits of both the complainant's case and the accused's defence, and must record brief reasons for its decision.
legal_tests_applied: The word “may” ordinarily does not mean “must” – Ordinarily, “may” will not be construed as “shall” – But this is not an inflexible rule – The use of the word “may” in certain legislations can be construed as “shall”, and the word “shall” can be construed as “may” – It all depends on the nature of the power conferred by the relevant provision of the statute and the effect of the exercise of the power.

To exercise the discretionary power under Section 143A, the Court will have to prima facie evaluate the merits of the case made out by the complainant and the merits of the defence pleaded by the accused in the reply to the application.
While deciding the prayer made under Section 143A, the Court must record brief reasons indicating consideration of all relevant factors.
The financial distress of the accused can also be a consideration.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's primary arguments were accepted by the court, leading to the appeal being partly allowed. The provided text does not contain any reasoning for why the appellant's position was not fully successful.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's argument that sub-section (1) of Section 143A is mandatory was rejected. The court held that the word 'may' signifies discretion, not a compulsion.

The respondent's submission that the defence of the accused is irrelevant at the interim stage was rejected. The court explicitly ruled that a prima facie evaluation of the defence pleaded by the accused is a necessary factor for the court to consider.

The respondent's argument that the presumption under Section 139 of the N.I. Act necessitates a mandatory order for interim compensation was not accepted, as the court prioritized a judicious exercise of discretionary power over an automatic application of the provision.
policy_considerations: The court acknowledged the legislative intent to address undue delays in cheque dishonour cases and the injustice caused to payees by unscrupulous drawers who prolong proceedings. The amendments were intended to strengthen the credibility of cheques and help trade and commerce.

The court distinguished the application of Section 143A from Section 148, noting that while the appellate court under Section 148 is normally justified in imposing a condition of deposit to curb frivolous appeals post-conviction, the power under Section 143A is exercised at a pre-conviction stage and thus requires a more careful, discretionary evaluation to avoid being unjust to the accused.
